correctness.rationale: The radial law is normalized expected volume (volume-weighted hulls), not the quenched uniform law. The Gaussian radius density gives the factor t^(d/2)/(2^(d/2-1)Γ(d/2)) times the unnormalized Mellin mass and the radial Laplace transform. The actual Gaussian-probe formulas were checked against Kabluchko (64)–(65) and the companion Theorem 5.1. Factoring the lowest power in each Ψ series gives the Beta((d+1)/2,1/2) mix in B and h(t/4)^d times the stated correction in A; for A use sinh(2 asinh(√t/2))=√t√(1+t/4). On a fixed small complex disk the factorial ratio series gives both corrections 1+O(|t|) uniformly. For the B mixing, E(1-U)^j≤(1/2)_j(2/d)^j, so E exp(Cd|t|(1-U))≤(1-2C|t|)^(-1/2); this bounds the error when replacing h(tU)^d by h(t)^d even for imaginary t. The logarithmic linear/quadratic coefficients are -1/6 and 11/180, or scaled by 1/4 and 1/16 for A. At t=-2is/√d, after centering these give variances 22/45 and 11/360. The bounded analytic log-error has bounded first two derivatives on a smaller fixed disk, proving the O(1) moment remainders as well; the exact moments follow from the first three terms of each normalized Ψ series. Independently, h(t)=∫_0^1(1+tx²)^(-1/2)dx is the Laplace transform at t/2 of U_0²Z² for independent uniform U_0 on [0,1] and scalar standard normal Z, whose first two moments are 1/3 and 3/5. This checks the two cumulants and the time-average squared-radius variance ratio 11/5 at leading order. The frozen rational checker was inspected, not executed; its finite checks are not evidence of distributional convergence by themselves.

value.rationale: This gives the distribution of fluctuations at the previously identified thin shells of two canonical volume-annealed Brownian hulls. It resolves shape, not just scale, and shows both have the same standardized variance, strictly higher than that of the matching Gaussian path-average proxy. The observable is useful for comparing interior mass distributions even though it does not answer quenched questions or provide a convergence rate.
